bigPicture.subtitle: The Lamb Has Overcome, and He Is Coming Soon
paragraphs: Picture an old man in exile on a rocky island in the Aegean Sea. He is the last of the twelve apostles still living. The churches he loves on the mainland are small and pressured: some are being slandered and imprisoned, some are drifting into compromise, some have grown comfortable and lukewarm. The empire around them is vast and confident, its emperor honoured as lord and god, its cities full of temples. On a Sunday, while he is worshipping, the old man hears a voice behind him like a trumpet — and turns to see the risen Jesus.

That is how the last book of the Bible begins: “This is the Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show to his servants the things which must happen soon” (Revelation 1:1). The word ‘Revelation’ is ἀποκάλυψις, an unveiling — the drawing back of a curtain. It is first a revelation of Jesus Christ Himself: the Son of Man among the lampstands, the Lamb who was slain and is standing, the Rider called Faithful and True. Then it unveils what is really happening behind the events of history: a throne in heaven that no earthly empire can shake, a war with the dragon already decided at the cross, and a future in which God dwells with His people in a new creation.

Revelation is written in a style called apocalyptic, full of symbols drawn from the Old Testament — lampstands, seals, trumpets, beasts, a woman, a city, a bride. The symbols are not a puzzle code for the clever; they are pictures that show the true nature of things. Rome looks like a glittering city; Revelation shows it as a prostitute drunk on the blood of the saints. The church looks small and weak; Revelation shows it as a vast multitude in white robes before the throne. Jesus looks defeated, crucified by Rome; Revelation shows Him as the Lion of Judah who has overcome — by being the slain Lamb.

The book says it was written by John (1:1, 4, 9; 22:8), and the early church identified him with the apostle John, the author of the Gospel and letters, writing from Patmos near the end of the first century, probably under the emperor Domitian (about AD 95). Some scholars think it was a different John, or date it earlier, under Nero; the book itself names only ‘John’. Christians have also read it in different ways: as describing events in the first century, as a map of church history, as mainly about the final events before Christ's return, or as a picture of the timeless battle between God and evil. This study will read each passage in the way that best fits its own words, and say honestly where faithful Christians disagree.

bridge.intro: 1 John ended by pointing ahead to 2 John and 3 John. Those two short letters are waiting for a full copy of their text, so this study now moves on to the last book written by the same John, and the last book of the Bible. The threads of 1 John run straight into Revelation.

points.title: From ‘You Have Overcome’ to ‘To Him Who Overcomes’
points.body: John wrote to the young men, “you have overcome the evil one” (1 John 2:13), and said, “This is the victory that has overcome the world: your faith” (1 John 5:4). In Revelation the same verb, νικάω, closes each of the seven letters: “To him who overcomes I will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the Paradise of my God” (Revelation 2:7). And the source of every victory is the Lamb: “Behold, the Lion who is of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has overcome” (Revelation 5:5).

points.title: From Antichrists to the Beast
points.body: 1 John warned that “even now many antichrists have arisen” (1 John 2:18), and spoke of “the spirit of the Antichrist, of whom you have heard that it comes” (1 John 4:3). Revelation unveils the full shape of that opposition: a dragon, a beast from the sea and a false prophet from the land, who deceive the world and demand its worship. The test is the same in both books: who do you confess Jesus to be, and whom do you worship?

points.title: From ‘Keep Yourselves from Idols’ to ‘Worship God’
points.body: 1 John ended, “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1 John 5:21). Revelation is a book about worship: the beast demands it, and the saints refuse it, even to death. When John himself falls at an angel's feet, he is told, “See you don’t do it! I am a fellow bondservant with you and with your brothers, the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God” (Revelation 22:9). And the first of the seven churches addressed is Ephesus, the city of Artemis (2:1).

points.title: From ‘We Will See Him’ to ‘They Will See His Face’
points.body: John promised, “when he is revealed, we will be like him; for we will see him just as he is” (1 John 3:2). Revelation ends with that promise fulfilled: “They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads” (Revelation 22:4). The true God of 1 John 5:20 is the One whose words are “faithful and true” (Revelation 21:5), and the eternal life John wrote about becomes a river of the water of life flowing from the throne.

coreTheme.title: The Lamb on the Throne — Overcome, for He Has Overcome
paragraphs: At the centre of Revelation is a throne. In chapter 4 John is taken up into heaven and sees God seated in majesty, surrounded by worship: “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty, who was and who is and who is to come!” (Revelation 4:8). Whatever is happening on earth — persecution, war, plague, deception — the throne is not empty and is not shaken. History is not out of control.

And at the centre of the throne is a Lamb. John is told to look for a Lion, and he turns and sees “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (Revelation 5:6). This is the heart of the book: God conquers evil not by brute force but by the self-giving death of His Son. The Lamb is worthy to open the scroll of history because He was slain and bought people for God by His blood. Everything that follows — seals, trumpets, bowls — flows from His hand.

So the call to the church is to overcome in the same way the Lamb did: by faithful witness, even to death. “They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death” (Revelation 12:11). The book promises that this costly faithfulness will be vindicated: “The kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord, and of his Christ. He will reign forever and ever!” (Revelation 11:15).

And it ends with the goal of the whole Bible: “Behold, God’s dwelling is with people, and he will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God” (Revelation 21:3). The story that began in a garden with a tree of life ends in a city with the tree of life, where there is no curse, no death, no tears — and the One on the throne says, “Behold, I am making all things new” (Revelation 21:5).

truths.intro: As we journey through these 22 chapters, the Holy Spirit wants to anchor these truths in your spirit:

items.title: Jesus Is Lord of History
items.body: Revelation opens with a vision of the risen Christ holding the stars in His hand and the keys of death in His power: “I was dead, and behold, I am alive forever and ever. Amen. I have the keys of Death and of Hades” (Revelation 1:18). No emperor, no beast, no disaster is outside His rule. Whatever your fear, it is not on the throne.

items.title: Faithful Witness Will Cost Something — and Win
items.body: Revelation never promises that believers will escape suffering. It promises that suffering faithfulness is victory. The Lamb's followers overcome “because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony” (Revelation 12:11). Compromise with the world's idols looks safe but loses everything; faithfulness looks costly but inherits everything.

items.title: He Is Coming, and All Things Will Be Made New
items.body: The book is not mainly about charts and dates but about a Person who is coming: “Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him” (Revelation 1:7). Evil will be judged, Babylon will fall, the devil will be thrown down, death will be destroyed, and God will dwell with His people forever. The church's answer is the Bible's last prayer: ‘Come, Lord Jesus.’

preparation.intro: Before we step into Chapter 1, prepare your spirit with these reflections:

items.title: Read for Worship, Not for Curiosity
items.body: Revelation promises a blessing: “Blessed is he who reads and those who hear the words of the prophecy, and keep the things that are written in it, for the time is at hand” (Revelation 1:3). The blessing is not for those who solve every symbol, but for those who keep its words. Ask the Spirit to show you Jesus, to lead you into worship, and to make you faithful.

items.title: Where Is Your Lampstand?
items.body: Jesus walks among the seven churches and knows each one: their love, their compromise, their suffering, their sleep. Before you begin, ask yourself which of the seven you most resemble — and invite the One with eyes like a flame of fire to speak to you as He spoke to them.

prayerOfActivation: “Lord Jesus Christ, faithful witness, firstborn of the dead and ruler of the kings of the earth, You love me and have freed me from my sins by Your blood, and made me part of Your kingdom and a priest to Your God and Father. To You be the glory and the dominion forever and ever. As I open the Revelation You gave to Your servant John, unveil Yourself to me. Let me see You walking among Your churches with eyes like fire, and let me fall at Your feet and hear You say, ‘Don’t be afraid.’ Lift my eyes to the throne in heaven, and let me see the Lamb who was slain and is worthy. Where I have left my first love, call me back. Where I have compromised with idols, make me faithful. Where I am lukewarm, set me on fire. Give me courage to overcome by Your blood and by the word of my testimony, even when it costs me. Keep me from the deceptions of the beast and the glitter of Babylon. Fill me with hope for the new heaven and the new earth, where You will wipe away every tear. Holy Spirit, let me hear what You are saying to the churches. Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.”
